paragraphs: This paper proposes a neural network layer that performs convolution-related computation in the Hadamard transform domain. Its mathematical starting point is a theorem connecting dyadic convolution of two vectors to element-by-element multiplication of their transformed representations. The resulting HT-perceptron layer provides a computationally cheaper alternative to a regular Conv2D layer.

The design also connects naturally to hybrid quantum-classical computing. Computing the Hadamard transform on a quantum computer requires applying a Hadamard gate separately to each qubit. This gives the transform operations in the proposed layer a quantum implementation, while the paper evaluates the layer through image classification networks.

On MNIST, the proposed network reaches 99.31% test accuracy, compared with 99.26% for a CNN with the same number of trainable parameters, while reducing multiply-accumulate operations by 57.1%. On ImageNet-1K, its modified ResNet-50 improves center-crop top-1 accuracy by 0.59 percentage points, with 11.5% fewer parameters and 12.6% fewer multiply-accumulate operations. These results show improved accuracy alongside reduced computational requirements in the reported comparisons.
icml-2023-a-hybrid-quantum-classical-app.tldr: A Hadamard-transform neural layer supports quantum implementation and improves reported image classification accuracy while reducing computation.

paragraphs: An optimization solver needs to recognize when a problem has no feasible solution, as well as find solutions when they exist. This paper studies how quickly first-order methods can detect such failures. The question matters for general-purpose solvers handling large problems, where infeasible or incorrectly specified inputs are part of the workload.

The analysis follows two quantities produced by fixed-point iterations: normalized iterates and fixed-point residuals. Both approach an object called the infimal displacement vector, which is central to the paper’s treatment of infeasibility detection. For standard iterations, the respective convergence rates are O(1/k²) and O(1/k), where k counts iterations. Acceleration retains the first rate and improves the residual rate to approximately O(1/k²), with logarithmic factors suppressed.

The authors also establish a matching complexity lower bound. This gives the accelerated rate a stronger interpretation than simply improving on one existing procedure: the stated Θ(1/k²) rate is optimal in the analyzed setting. The contribution provides a formal efficiency benchmark for infeasibility detection within first-order optimization.
icml-2023-accelerated-infeasibility-dete.tldr: The paper establishes an optimal accelerated rate for detecting infeasibility through first-order fixed-point methods.

paragraphs: GFlowNets build objects through sequences of decisions and learn to sample completed objects in proportion to their rewards. When a reward appears only at the end, training must work out which earlier decisions deserve credit. Longer sequences make this harder, and previous GFlowNet methods could not learn from sequences that stopped before a terminal reward was available.

This paper considers a specific opportunity: the energy function can also be evaluated at intermediate states. An additive energy, whose terms become available as construction proceeds, is one example. The authors change the parameterization of the state flow function so it incorporates the partial reward already accumulated. This produces a training objective that can update the model using incomplete trajectories.

Intermediate information also helps when complete trajectories are available. By making credit and gradients more local to the relevant decisions, the method speeds up convergence across the reported simulations. The central advance is therefore a way to use available partial reward information both to expand which trajectories support learning and to make learning from finished trajectories more efficient.
icml-2023-better-training-of-gflownets-w.tldr: When intermediate energies are available, GFlowNets can learn from unfinished trajectories and converge faster through more local credit assignment.

paragraphs: Many graph clustering methods assume that connected nodes tend to belong to similar groups, a property called homophily. Graphs with connections between unlike nodes challenge that assumption. In an unlabeled clustering problem, the authors argue that one cannot first identify the graph’s homophily type and then choose an appropriate model, motivating a method that accommodates different connection patterns.

Their method reconstructs two graphs from each dataset: one with high homophily and one with high heterophily. A mixed filter uses these structures to extract both low-frequency and high-frequency information, capturing different patterns of variation across nodes. A dual clustering network then maps node attributes and graph structure into separate subspaces to reduce harmful coupling between those information sources.

Experiments cover 11 benchmark graphs and report promising overall performance, with particularly strong results on heterophilic graphs. The approach matters because it builds multiple views of connectivity into the clustering process instead of relying on one homophily assumption. The findings support this reconstruction-and-filtering strategy across the tested graphs, especially where conventional similarity-based connections are a poor fit.
icml-2023-beyond-homophily-reconstructin.tldr: Reconstructing complementary graph structures helps cluster nodes across different homophily levels, with especially strong reported results on heterophilic graphs.

paragraphs: An agent learning without external supervision needs a reason to discover behaviors beyond those it already finds easy. Existing unsupervised skill discovery methods often settle on simple skills because they lack an incentive to pursue more challenging ones. This paper introduces Controllability-aware Skill Discovery, or CSD, to make that incentive depend on the agent’s evolving abilities.

CSD learns a distance function that gives larger values to state transitions that are difficult to achieve with the current skills. The skill-learning process seeks to maximize this distance. Because the distance function is trained jointly with the skills, transitions that become easy receive less reward, directing learning toward progressively harder behaviors.

The authors evaluate CSD in six robotic manipulation and locomotion environments. They report diverse, complex skills learned without supervision, including object manipulation and locomotion, and significant improvements over prior unsupervised skill discovery methods. The findings support an adaptive approach to exploration: what counts as a rewarding discovery changes as the agent becomes more capable, helping it move beyond repeatedly practicing easy behaviors.
icml-2023-controllability-aware-unsuperv.tldr: CSD rewards transitions that current skills find difficult, enabling progressively more complex unsupervised behaviors in robotic environments.

paragraphs: Training with differential privacy can reduce a neural network’s predictive performance. This paper examines that problem through the geometry of the training objective, focusing on sharpness. The authors show that flat minima can lessen the harmful effects of two operations used in private learning: clipping each example’s gradient and adding Gaussian noise.

They then investigate Sharpness-Aware Minimization, or SAM, as a way to find flatter minima. SAM proves useful for this purpose in private learning, but its two-step optimization creates additional costs in both computation and privacy budget. Thus, a method that improves the optimization landscape can also make private training more expensive along other dimensions.

To address this tension, the authors propose a new sharpness-aware training method that mitigates the trade-off between privacy and optimization. Experiments report performance improvements for differentially private models trained both from scratch and through fine-tuning. The contribution connects a geometric explanation of private training difficulties to a practical training approach, while explicitly accounting for the costs introduced by the original sharpness-aware procedure.
icml-2023-differentially-private-sharpne.tldr: A new sharpness-aware training method improves differentially private learning while mitigating SAM’s privacy-budget and computational costs.

paragraphs: Reward-driven agents may learn to pursue success through deception, power-seeking, or other harmful behavior. This paper introduces Machiavelli, a benchmark designed to measure those tendencies in socially rich decision-making settings. It contains 134 Choose-Your-Own-Adventure games and more than half a million scenarios, giving agents many opportunities to choose between different ways of achieving goals.

The authors formalize dozens of harmful behaviors and use language models to annotate scenarios automatically. They report that these models outperform human annotators for the labeling task. The annotations support measurements of power-seeking, harm to others, and ethical violations, allowing the evaluation to examine how an agent earns rewards as well as how much reward it earns.

The experiments reveal some tension between maximizing reward and behaving ethically. However, language-model-based steering methods improve the trade-off, showing that competence and more ethical behavior can coexist in the evaluated settings. The reported Pareto improvements mean that safety and capability can improve together, supporting concrete progress on machine ethics rather than treating every reduction in harm as an unavoidable loss of performance.
icml-2023-do-the-rewards-justify-the-mea.tldr: Machiavelli measures harmful behavior in game-playing agents and shows that steering can improve both ethical behavior and competence.

paragraphs: This paper asks when multiple machines benefit from collaborating on an online optimization problem. The machines work in parallel, communicate intermittently, and face convex costs that an adaptive adversary can generate. The objective is to minimize average regret, measuring the cost of their sequential decisions relative to a comparison decision.

The answer depends on the feedback available. When each machine receives gradient information at its queried points, the authors find that collaboration is not beneficial in this adaptive setting. This differs from the stochastic setting, where cost functions are sampled from a fixed distribution. When machines receive only function values, the authors identify a high-dimensional regime where collaboration helps and may provide speedup linear in the number of machines.

The paper also develops distributed algorithms for adversarial linear bandits with single-point and two-point feedback. Tight regret bounds cover both gradient and function-value feedback under intermittent communication. Together, these results clarify why the benefits of federated optimization depend on both the information returned by each query and whether the sequence of costs can adapt.
icml-2023-federated-online-and-bandit-co.tldr: Under adaptive convex costs, collaboration offers no benefit with gradient feedback but can yield linear speedup in a high-dimensional bandit regime.

paragraphs: Federated learning must handle differences between clients’ data as well as changes in those data over time. Adaptive optimizers can address the first problem, called statistical heterogeneity, but may react slowly to concept drift. Flash is an adaptive optimizer designed to address both problems within the same training process.

Its central insight is that the size of a client’s parameter updates can signal a change in the local data distribution. If fitting the shared model to local data requires substantial adjustment, that update magnitude provides evidence relevant to drift detection. Flash combines early stopping during client training, which facilitates detection, with a server-side optimizer that adjusts the effective learning rate in response to drift.

The authors prove that Flash matches the convergence rate of state-of-the-art adaptive optimizers and evaluate it across federated learning benchmarks with different drift settings. The contribution links detection and response: client training provides a drift-sensitive signal, and server optimization uses that signal to adapt. The theoretical result establishes convergence-rate parity while the experiments examine the method’s behavior under changing data.
icml-2023-flash-concept-drift-adaptation.tldr: Flash combines client-side drift detection with server-side adaptive learning rates to address heterogeneous and changing federated data.

paragraphs: Compositional datasets describe components of a whole and can contain many variables and many zeros. Reducing their dimension is difficult because common log-ratio transformations do not handle zeros naturally, while some alternatives sacrifice interpretability. This paper develops a method for finding a smaller, informative representation of such data.

The approach uses sufficient dimension reduction, which seeks a representation that retains the information needed to relate the inputs to a response. Once that representation is known, the original inputs should provide no additional response information in the framework’s conditional-independence sense. The proposed compositional version handles zeros and accounts for nonlinear relationships and spurious negative correlations between components. It also examines variable selection through sub-compositions and amalgamation, or combining components.

The authors establish statistical consistency for constructing a smaller compositional space containing true signal variables. Simulations and real microbiome data compare the method with existing approaches. The contribution brings prediction-relevant dimension reduction and interpretable variable selection into a setting where zeros and the relationships imposed by composition make ordinary transformations problematic.
icml-2023-kernel-sufficient-dimension-re.tldr: A compositional dimension-reduction method handles zeros and nonlinear structure while consistently identifying a smaller space of signal variables.

paragraphs: Evidential deep learning lets a deterministic neural network represent uncertainty through learned evidence. For the underlying theory to remain valid, that evidence must be non-negative, so the network uses special activation functions. Yet these models often predict less accurately than standard softmax models, making them harder to apply to large datasets.

The paper investigates why this performance gap occurs. Its theoretical analysis identifies regions created by existing evidential activations where the model produces zero evidence and cannot learn from training samples falling there. This connects the loss of predictive performance to a specific failure of the learning process: some examples fail to contribute useful learning because of how evidence is constrained.

Using that analysis, the authors design a regularizer that alleviates the zero-evidence limitation. Experiments across challenging real-world datasets and settings support the theoretical findings and demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The work matters because it addresses a concrete obstacle inside evidential training, offering a route to better prediction while retaining the framework’s requirement that evidence remain non-negative.
icml-2023-learn-to-accumulate-evidence-f.tldr: The paper identifies zero-evidence regions that block evidential learning and introduces a regularizer that alleviates the problem.

paragraphs: Spatial propagation tasks use relationships between image locations to guide how information moves across an image. This paper focuses on learning those relationships, or affinities, with a representation that captures hierarchy. It draws on hyperbolic geometry because that geometry has shown value for representing hierarchical relationships in learned features.

The authors introduce a Hyperbolic Affinity learning Module, called HAM. The module measures spatial affinity using geodesic distance in hyperbolic space, meaning distance is evaluated within the chosen geometry. This makes the geometry part of how the model represents relationships between pixels. HAM can be incorporated into conventional spatial propagation methods, giving those methods a way to learn hierarchical affinity maps.

The reported evaluations validate the module’s effectiveness in capturing pixel hierarchy and show that it can improve explicit propagation tasks, including depth completion and semantic segmentation. The contribution is a reusable affinity-learning component: it changes how relationships are represented within a propagation process. The findings support hyperbolic representation as a useful option for these tasks, with performance improvements possible through integration into existing methods.
icml-2023-learning-affinity-with-hyperbo.tldr: HAM uses hyperbolic distances to learn hierarchical pixel affinities and can improve depth completion and semantic segmentation.

paragraphs: Super-resolution models trained on simple synthetic downscaling may struggle with real low-resolution images. Real degradation can include noise, blur, and color distortion, and those effects change with the downscaling factor. Collecting realistic training pairs takes substantial effort, so available datasets often cover only a few factors.

This paper proposes generating additional realistic training data at previously unseen degradation levels. The approach explores the latent space of real low-resolution images to produce a wider variety of degraded images while preserving complex real-world artifacts. The intended benefit is broader coverage of realistic degradation without collecting a separate dataset for every level.

Quantitative and visual experiments support the accuracy of the generated low-resolution images. The authors also train several conventional super-resolution networks on the new datasets and report substantially better high-resolution outputs. This second result connects the quality of the generated data to its practical training value. The contribution therefore improves super-resolution through the examples used to train models, with the generated degradation diversity benefiting multiple existing network designs.
icml-2023-learning-controllable-degradat.tldr: Generating realistic low-resolution images at unseen degradation levels improves training data and the outputs of conventional super-resolution networks.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning can estimate policy gradients in two ways: using likelihood-ratio estimators or differentiating through a model with reparameterization gradients. Earlier Total Propagation work combined both using inverse-variance weighting and reported large improvements. The unresolved issue was whether this combination could scale to modern reinforcement learning tasks.

The paper introduces Total Propagation X, or TPX. It changes the node at which inverse-variance weighting is performed and uses separate weights for individual coordinates. These changes make the composite estimator scalable enough to integrate with Dreamer, a visual model-based reinforcement learning algorithm. The method retains the idea of combining gradient estimates according to their variability.

In the reported experiments, Dreamer fails with long simulation horizons, while the TPX version works reliably with a modest amount of additional computation. This demonstrates the practical value of the scalable combination in a demanding setting where predictions extend over many simulated steps. The authors also emphasize ease of implementation, positioning TPX as a way to make further experiments with inverse-variance-weighted estimators more accessible.
icml-2023-model-based-reinforcement-lear.tldr: TPX scales combined policy-gradient estimators and makes Dreamer reliable at long simulation horizons in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Neural differential equations offer ways to model time-varying data, including settings with irregular observation times or missing measurements. This paper develops a framework based on stochastic differential games, treating time-series analysis as a problem involving interacting neural agents. The motivation is to use their collective interaction to improve the modeling of temporal dynamics.

To train the framework, the authors introduce deep neural fictitious play, a gradient-descent-based algorithm that approximates a Nash equilibrium. They analyze its convergence theoretically and discuss how cooperative games help handle observations that provide little useful information. Cooperation is therefore part of both the modeling approach and the explanation for its predictive benefits.

Across experiments on multiple datasets, the framework outperforms all tested comparison methods in time-series prediction. An ablation study further indicates that its neural agents learn intrinsic temporal relevance, supporting the proposed account of how accurate predictions arise. The findings provide empirical evidence for the cooperative game formulation within the tested settings, alongside a theoretical analysis of the algorithm used to train it.
icml-2023-neural-stochastic-differential.tldr: A cooperative stochastic-game framework trains interacting neural agents and improves time-series prediction over the tested comparison methods.

paragraphs: An invariant representation transforms input variables so that the best predictor built on it stays the same across training environments. Such representations might support prediction under changes to the system that generated the data. This paper studies that possibility for linear structural equation models, where different environments arise through interventions.

The authors focus on finite data, introducing approximate invariance with a tolerance called epsilon. Their central question is whether a representation that is approximately invariant across a given collection of training interventions will preserve that property across a larger collection of unseen interventions. This frames generalization around the stability of the representation’s predictive relationship across environments.

Drawing on probably approximately correct learning, the paper obtains finite-sample guarantees that hold probabilistically over a family of linear structural equation models. The results do not require faithfulness assumptions. Their significance lies in giving approximate invariance an out-of-distribution generalization framework with explicit statistical scope: the guarantee concerns a probability statement over the studied model family, rather than certainty for every possible intervention.
icml-2023-pac-generalization-via-invaria.tldr: The paper gives probabilistic finite-sample guarantees for approximate invariance across unseen interventions in linear structural equation models.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning relies on predicting what actions will do. In complex environments, inaccurate predictions can undermine the controller that plans with them. Predictable MDP Abstraction, or PMA, addresses this difficulty by changing the decision process on which the predictive model is trained.

PMA learns a transformed action space that permits predictable, easier-to-model actions while covering as much of the original state-action space as possible. This creates a balance between making prediction manageable and retaining broad access to the environment. The transformation is learned without supervision and before a user specifies a task, so the learned abstraction is prepared for later control problems.

Downstream tasks can then be solved through model-based control without additional environment interactions. The authors provide theoretical analysis and report significant improvements over prior unsupervised model-based reinforcement learning approaches across benchmark environments. The approach matters because it makes predictability part of the action representation itself. Easier and more accurate model learning can then support robust, stable planning within the transformed decision process.
icml-2023-predictable-mdp-abstraction-fo.tldr: PMA learns a predictable action space before tasks are specified, enabling improved model-based control without further environment interactions.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks for three-dimensional data often need their outputs and internal representations to transform consistently when the input rotates. This property is called rotation equivariance. Achieving it becomes computationally expensive when networks use higher-order tensor representations, because the required equivariant convolutions grow rapidly in complexity.

The paper shows how to replace SO(3) convolutions or tensor products with mathematically equivalent SO(2) convolutions. It does this by aligning the primary axis of node embeddings with graph edge vectors. In that coordinate alignment, the tensor product becomes sparse, reducing the computational complexity from O(L⁶) to O(L³), where L is the degree of the representation.

The authors build this operation into the Equivariant Spherical Channel Network, or eSCN. They report state-of-the-art results on the large-scale OC-20 and OC-22 datasets. The mathematical equivalence is central: the computational saving comes from reformulating the equivariant operation. The experiments then demonstrate the usefulness of that reformulation inside a complete graph neural network for three-dimensional data.
icml-2023-reducing-so-3-convolutions-to-.tldr: An equivalent SO(2) formulation reduces rotation-equivariant convolution complexity from O(L⁶) to O(L³) and powers strong eSCN results.

paragraphs: Computing statistics across distributed clients requires a way to combine their information while protecting individual contributions. This paper introduces FED-χ², a federated correlation-testing framework compatible with secure aggregation. The design makes the statistical calculation fit an aggregation procedure that conceals each client’s update.

The authors reformulate the computation as frequency-moment estimation. Clients jointly generate a shared projection matrix and use stable projections to encode local information into compact vectors. Those vectors can be added together, which is the key property enabling secure aggregation. The paper proves a security guarantee that the server learns only the minimum required information, namely the correlation statistics.

The same construction can extend to other statistics expressible through frequency-moment estimation. Applying it to Shannon entropy yields FED-H, a secure federated entropy-estimation protocol. Evaluations in several real-world case studies report good performance with small client-side computational overhead. The contribution combines a formally analyzed information guarantee with compact, aggregatable representations, allowing useful statistical calculations without exposing individual client updates.
icml-2023-secure-federated-correlation-t.tldr: FED-χ² and FED-H use compact, securely aggregatable projections for federated correlation testing and entropy estimation.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning in congestion games under semi-bandit feedback, where participants receive limited information about their decisions. The authors propose a variant of online stochastic gradient descent and prove two properties together: convergence to Nash equilibria and sublinear regret. The latter means accumulated regret grows more slowly than the number of rounds.

A central issue is that the number of possible actions can be exponentially large relative to the number of facilities. The proposed method’s convergence rates depend polynomially on the numbers of players and facilities, without depending on the action-set size. Its running time is also polynomial in the game’s implicit description, making compact problem structure important to the result.

The analysis combines ideas from convex geometry, including Carathéodory’s theorem, with advances in non-convex stochastic optimization. The contribution is a joint guarantee: players can approach equilibrium while also controlling their learning regret under limited feedback. The scaling results show that these guarantees need not carry an explicit dependence on an exponentially large list of actions.
icml-2023-semi-bandit-dynamics-in-conges.tldr: A stochastic-gradient learning rule achieves equilibrium convergence and sublinear regret in congestion games without scaling with action-set size.

paragraphs: Representational drift occurs when a network’s internal activations change over time while its task performance remains stable. This paper investigates how noise from stochastic gradient descent can produce that behavior. The authors use theory and simulations in a two-layer linear feedforward network undergoing continual online learning, motivated by experimental observations of stimulus-dependent drift in the brain.

They separate learning dynamics into motion perpendicular to and along the set of minimum-loss solutions. Perpendicular motion produces fluctuations with finite variance. Motion along the set can be viewed as an effective diffusion process, allowing internal representations to move while remaining associated with minimum-loss solutions. This decomposition distinguishes two effects of the same noisy learning dynamics.

The authors analytically calculate fluctuation and diffusion coefficients for hidden-layer stimulus representations as functions of network parameters and the input distribution. They also find slower drift for stimuli presented more frequently, consistent with the motivating experiments. The result provides a theoretical mechanism for stable performance alongside changing representations within the studied linear network.
icml-2023-stochastic-gradient-descent-in.tldr: In a two-layer linear network, SGD noise produces representational diffusion, with more frequently presented stimuli drifting more slowly.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning gives a language model task-specific abilities, but it is less clear where the relevant changes reside. This paper studies skill localization by identifying a very small subset of parameters whose fine-tuned values preserve most task performance when transferred back into the original pretrained model.

A simple optimization finds subsets containing approximately 0.01% of model parameters that account for more than 95% of fine-tuned performance in this grafting sense. The selected parameters require no further retraining. The authors also report improved in-distribution calibration, with calibration-error reductions of 40–90%, and better out-of-distribution predictions compared with ordinary fine-tuning.

For models trained on multiple tasks, the localized parameter regions are almost disjoint. Where regions overlap, that overlap acts as a proxy for task similarity. Experiments further suggest that grafting can help certain forms of continual learning. These findings give an operational meaning to localized skills: a small set of transferred parameter values can recover much of a task’s performance, while relationships between those sets provide information about relationships between tasks.
icml-2023-task-specific-skill-localizati.tldr: Grafting roughly 0.01% of fine-tuned parameters preserves over 95% of task performance and can improve calibration and out-of-distribution prediction.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks a model to work in a target domain that was unknown during training. A major difficulty is that test examples may have styles far from those seen in the source domains. This paper addresses that mismatch by changing the style of an incoming example before the model makes its prediction.

The proposed test-time style shifting moves a sample with a large style gap toward the nearest source domain familiar to the model. It requires no model update at test time. The authors also introduce style balancing to address imbalance issues specific to domain generalization, creating better conditions for style shifting to help.

The methods are described as easy to implement and compatible with various other domain-generalization approaches. Experiments on different datasets demonstrate their effectiveness. The core idea is to handle unfamiliar style statistics through a transformation of the test input, using known source styles as reference points. Style balancing complements this by addressing the training-side imbalance that affects how much benefit the shift can provide.
icml-2023-test-time-style-shifting-handl.tldr: Shifting unfamiliar test styles toward known source domains improves domain generalization without updating the model at test time.

paragraphs: Federated learning can share information by distilling an ensemble of client models on an unlabeled public dataset. Although this approach has shown experimental value, its theoretical foundations were less developed. This paper studies ensemble distillation through kernel ridge regression, providing a setting in which its generalization behavior can be analyzed.

The authors propose a distillation-based federated algorithm for kernel ridge regression models and relate it to existing federated distillation methods. Their main result compares the local models with a centralized kernel ridge regression model trained on all clients’ datasets. If the unlabeled public dataset is sufficiently large, the local models match the centralized model’s convergence rate for generalization error.

That condition makes the public dataset central to the guarantee. The conclusion concerns the rate at which generalization error converges, giving a precise meaning to the local models reaching centralized statistical performance in this analysis. Experiments support the theoretical results. The paper thereby explains how ensemble distillation can transfer enough shared information to obtain a centralized convergence rate within the studied kernel regression framework.
icml-2023-towards-understanding-ensemble.tldr: With sufficiently many unlabeled public examples, federated ensemble distillation matches centralized kernel ridge regression’s generalization-error convergence rate.

paragraphs: Data attribution seeks to connect a model’s predictions to its training examples. Existing methods often face a practical trade-off: computationally manageable approaches may give poor attributions for non-convex models, while effective alternatives can require training thousands of models. That cost makes attribution difficult for large networks and datasets.

TRAK, short for Tracing with the Randomly-projected After Kernel, is designed to make effective attribution computationally practical for large differentiable models. The authors report that it can match attribution methods requiring thousands of trained models while using only a handful. This reduces the model-training burden associated with obtaining useful attribution results.

The paper demonstrates TRAK across ImageNet image classifiers, CLIP vision-language models, and the BERT and mT5 language models. These examples show its utility across multiple modalities and model scales. The central finding is that effective training-data attribution can be made substantially more tractable in the evaluated settings, allowing the connection between training examples and model predictions to be studied without the previously prohibitive number of training runs.
icml-2023-trak-attributing-model-behavio.tldr: TRAK attributes predictions to training data using only a handful of models while matching methods that require thousands.
